## Proof

**Theorem (Borel, 1895).** For every sequence of real numbers $\{a_k\}_{k \geq 1}$ there exists $f \in C^\infty\bigl((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon),\mathbb{R}\bigr)$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ such that $f^{(k)}(0)=a_k$ for all $k\geq 1$.

In fact we prove the stronger statement that *all* derivatives (including order $0$) can be prescribed arbitrarily.

---

### Setup

Let $\{c_k\}_{k\geq 0}$ be an arbitrary real sequence (we will later take $c_0=0$ and $c_k=a_k$ for $k\geq 1$). Choose a bump function $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ with

$$\psi(x)=1 \text{ for } |x|\leq 1, \qquad \operatorname{supp}\psi\subset[-1,1].$$

For each $k\geq 0$ and a parameter $\varepsilon_k>0$ to be chosen, define

$$g_k(x) \;=\; \frac{c_k}{k!}\,x^{k}\,\psi\!\Bigl(\frac{x}{\varepsilon_k}\Bigr).$$

**Key local property.** Since $\psi\equiv 1$ on $[-1,1]$, on the interval $|x|<\varepsilon_k$ we have $g_k(x)=\frac{c_k}{k!}x^k$. Consequently

$$g_k^{(j)}(0)=\begin{cases} c_k & j=k,\\[2pt] 0 & j\neq k.\end{cases} \tag{$\ast$}$$

### Choosing $\varepsilon_k$

We claim $\varepsilon_k>0$ can be chosen so that, simultaneously for every $j<k$,

$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} \bigl|g_k^{(j)}(x)\bigr| \;<\; 2^{-k}. \tag{$\dagger$}$$

To see this, bound the derivatives. By Leibniz,

$$g_k^{(j)}(x)=\frac{c_k}{k!}\sum_{m=0}^{\min(j,k)}\binom{j}{m}\frac{k!}{(k-m)!}\,x^{k-m}\,\varepsilon_k^{-(j-m)}\,\psi^{(j-m)}\!\Bigl(\frac{x}{\varepsilon_k}\Bigr).$$

The factor $\psi^{(j-m)}(x/\varepsilon_k)$ vanishes outside $|x|\leq\varepsilon_k$, and on that region $|x|^{k-m}\leq \varepsilon_k^{\,k-m}$. Setting $M_r:=\|\psi^{(r)}\|_\infty$, we get

$$\bigl|g_k^{(j)}(x)\bigr|\;\le\; |c_k|\sum_{m=0}^{\min(j,k)}\binom{j}{m}\frac{1}{(k-m)!}\,M_{j-m}\,\varepsilon_k^{\,k-j}.$$

For $j<k$ the exponent $k-j\geq 1$, so the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $\varepsilon_k\to 0^+$. For each fixed $k$ there are only finitely many constraints $j=0,1,\dots,k-1$; taking $\varepsilon_k$ smaller than the minimum of the finitely many thresholds required gives $(\dagger)$. We also take $\varepsilon_k<1$ for tidiness.

### Convergence in $C^\infty$

Define $f(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} g_k(x)$. Fix any $j\geq 0$ and split

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} g_k^{(j)} \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{j} g_k^{(j)}}_{\text{finite sum of }C^\infty\text{ functions}} \;+\; \sum_{k=j+1}^{\infty} g_k^{(j)}.$$

For $k>j$ we have $j<k$, so by $(\dagger)$, $\sup|g_k^{(j)}|<2^{-k}$. The tail is thus dominated by $\sum_{k>j}2^{-k}$, which converges. By the Weierstrass $M$-test, $\sum_k g_k^{(j)}$ converges **uniformly** on $\mathbb{R}$ for every $j$. A standard induction (uniform convergence of each derivative series) then gives $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ with

$$f^{(j)}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}g_k^{(j)}(x),\qquad\text{all }j.$$

### Evaluating at the origin

Using $(\ast)$ and termwise differentiation at $0$ (justified by uniform convergence of the derivative series near $0$),

$$f^{(j)}(0)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}g_k^{(j)}(0)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_k\,\delta_{jk}=c_j,\qquad j=0,1,2,\dots$$

### Applying to the given problem

Set $c_0:=0$ (arbitrary, since $f(0)$ is unconstrained) and $c_k:=a_k$ for $k\geq 1$. The construction yields $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ with

$$f^{(k)}(0)=a_k\qquad\text{for every }k\geq 1.$$

Restricting $f$ to any interval $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon>0$ (e.g. $\varepsilon=1$) gives the desired smooth function on a neighborhood of $0$.

$\blacksquare$
